sections.title: Hidden layers hold patterns, not sentences
paragraphs: Inside a trained {{model}}, each layer turns {{input}} numbers into new numbers. Those intermediate lists are representations: compressed patterns the network found useful for the {{target}}.
An {{embedding}} is a representation stored as a vector: a fixed-length list of numbers. Similar meanings tend to land in nearby regions of that space.
You do not read an {{embedding}} like a paragraph. You compare vectors (for example with angles or distances) to see which items the inside of the {{model}} treats as alike.
In a tiny classifier, the hidden layer already builds a representation before the final scores. In language models, each {{token}} usually begins as an {{embedding}} lookup.
This lesson stays inside the network. Later retrieval products reuse embeddings to search documents; the maths of "nearby means similar" starts here.
bullets: Representation: internal number pattern for an {{input}}.
{{embedding}}: a vector used as that pattern.

check.prompt: Two product titles land almost on top of each other in embedding space. What does that suggest inside the model?
check.answer: The model treats their meanings as similar
choices: The model treats their meanings as similar
The titles must share identical characters only
Embeddings store full PDF files uncompressed
The learning rate was set to zero
check.explanation: Embeddings place related items nearby. Close vectors are the inside signal that the {{model}} sees similar meaning, not a promise about spelling alone.

sections.title: From table lookup to layered geometry
paragraphs: Many language stacks begin with a table: each {{token}} id selects a row of numbers. That row is the token's {{embedding}} before deeper layers mix context.
Deeper layers transform those vectors with {{weights}}, {{bias}} and {{activation}}s. Attention (you will revisit it under Transformers) mixes information across positions.
After training, geometry in representation space reflects the {{dataset}}. If your labels never separate two concepts, do not expect clean clusters for them.
Click each idea. Keep the honesty bar: teaching diagrams use 2D arrows; production embeddings may have hundreds or thousands of dimensions.
When AiEval later compares answers, you still judge text on the outside. Representations explain why two phrasings can feel synonymous to a {{model}} even when strings differ.

reveals.prompt: Token id 17 → row 17 in a matrix.
reveals.reveal: That row is the starting {{embedding}} for the {{token}} before contextual layers run.

reveals.prompt: Two paraphrases embed nearby; a random string sits far away.
reveals.reveal: Useful geometry: meaning clusters, noise stays distant.

reveals.prompt: You only train on sports text.
reveals.reveal: Expect weak structure for legal jargon. Representations mirror the {{dataset}}.

check.prompt: Your hub diagram shows 2D dots for embeddings. What should you remember?
check.answer: Real embedding vectors usually have many more dimensions
choices: Real embedding vectors usually have many more dimensions
Production models only ever use 2 dimensions
Embeddings are the same as rubric scores
2D means the model cannot classify anything
check.explanation: Teaching plots flatten space so you can see clusters. Inside real models, {{embedding}} vectors are high-dimensional even when the idea of "nearby means similar" stays the same.

sections.title: Bridge to data literacy
paragraphs: Representations are only as trustworthy as the examples that shaped them. Messy labels and leakage show up as weird geometry and brittle {{prediction}}s.
Before you chase a fancier architecture, ask what the {{dataset}} teaches the inside of the {{model}} to treat as close.
Data literacy is next: distributions, leakage and which labels are worth collecting so representations have something honest to learn.
Side path reminder: Decision trees offer readable rules instead of dense vectors. They sit off the neural spine as optional practice from Data literacy.
Next lesson: **Data literacy**. Carry the idea that inside similarity is learned, not magical.
bullets: Optional side path later: Decision trees.

check.prompt: In a short phrase, what do embeddings mainly give the inside of a model?
accept: a space where nearby means alike
check.explanation: An {{embedding}} is an internal numeric pattern. The useful property is similarity: related {{input}}s land nearby so later layers (or retrieval tools) can use that geometry.

recapQuestions.prompt: Where do token embeddings usually enter a language model?
recapQuestions.answer: As a lookup row for each token before deeper layers
choices: As a lookup row for each token before deeper layers
Only after the judge JSON is parsed
As a replacement for the learning rate
recapQuestions.explanation: A common inside path is {{token}} id → {{embedding}} row → contextual layers. That is how text becomes numbers the network can transform.

recapQuestions.prompt: Complete: if two concepts never appear as distinct in training labels…
accept: the model may treat them alike
recapQuestions.explanation: Representations mirror the {{dataset}}. If labels never teach a split, inside geometry often keeps the concepts tangled.
